title: Starting a Small Business
summary: Learn how to spot a problem worth solving, test an idea cheaply, understand costs and pricing, and work out your break-even point. Includes simple marketing, record keeping and getting help.
audience: Students and young people who want to start or run a small business

body.p: Every lasting business begins with a problem that people already have and will pay to fix. A tailor fixes the problem of clothes that do not fit. A phone-charging stand fixes the problem of a flat battery in a place with unreliable electricity. The idea does not need to be new. It needs to be useful, and you need to know exactly who it is useful for.

list: Your own frustrations: what do you often wish was easier, cheaper or closer?
Complaints you hear: at the market, at school, at home, on the bus.
Waste: things people throw away that someone else could use, or time people lose queuing.
Skills you already have: cooking, braiding, repairing phones, graphic design, tutoring, farming.

body.p: A customer is a real group of people, not 'everybody'. Write one sentence: 'My customer is [who], who has [problem], and now solves it by [current way].' For example: 'Final-year students in my hostel who need documents printed late at night and now walk 20 minutes to a shop that closes at 6 pm.' The sentence tells you where to sell, when to open and what to charge.

body.h: Test the idea cheaply before you spend

body.p: Before you rent a shop or buy stock, find out whether people will really buy. Saying 'nice idea' costs nothing; handing over money does. Three cheap tests are: ask ten likely customers what they do now and what they pay; offer a small trial (one batch, one weekend); or take pre-orders and ask for a small deposit.

Worked example: you plan to sell snack boxes. You ask 20 students and 14 say they would buy at your price. That is 14 / 20 = 70% saying yes. Treat this carefully: people are polite and friends say yes to be kind, so the number of people who actually pay in a trial is usually lower. Run a trial of 30 boxes and count real sales before you invest more.

steps: Talk to 10 people in that group and note what they say, in their words.
Sell a small trial and record how many bought and what they said.
Decide: continue, change the idea, or stop. Stopping early with little lost is a success, not a failure.

body.tip: Keep your first version small. A business you can start with money you already have teaches you more than one that needs a big loan.

body.p: To know whether a business makes money you must know what it costs. Costs fall into two kinds. Variable costs change with how much you make or sell: ingredients, packaging, fuel for deliveries, goods bought for resale. Make nothing, and these are zero. Fixed costs stay the same each month whatever you sell: rent, a worker's agreed wage, a monthly phone or internet plan, a licence fee.

body.h: Worked example: a small bakery (amounts in naira)

body.p: One loaf needs flour 300, yeast 40, sugar 60, cooking fuel 80 and a bag 20. The variable cost per loaf is 300 + 40 + 60 + 80 + 20 = 500 naira. Fixed costs each month are rent 18,000, a helper's wage 12,000 and phone 3,000, which is 33,000 naira.

body.code:
Loaves baked in a month: 200
Variable cost: 200 x 500 = 100,000
Fixed cost:    33,000
Total cost:    133,000
Cost per loaf: 133,000 / 200 = 665

body.p: Notice that cost per loaf (665) is higher than the variable cost (500) because each loaf carries a share of the fixed costs. If you bake more loaves, the fixed cost is shared across more units and the cost per loaf falls. That is why many businesses want to grow, as long as customers are there to buy.

list: Your own time. If you work 8 hours a day, decide what that time is worth.
Waste and spoilage: bread that does not sell, fruit that rots, broken items.
Transport to buy stock.
Replacing equipment that wears out.
Unpaid credit: customers who take goods and pay late or never.

body.tip: Write every cost in two columns, fixed and variable. If you are unsure, ask: 'If I sold nothing this month, would I still pay this?' If yes, it is fixed.

body.p: Always check which costs apply in your country, such as business registration fees or local levies. Ask your local business office or a trusted adviser rather than guessing.

Price is what the customer pays. Profit is what is left after you subtract costs. A price that feels friendly to customers can still lose you money if you have not counted every cost. Three things set a good price: your costs (the lowest sensible price), what customers can and will pay, and what competitors charge.
Markup is profit as a percentage of cost. Margin is profit as a percentage of the selling price. People mix them up and then price wrongly, so learn the difference.

The same 200 profit is a 33.3% markup but only a 25% margin. If someone says 'I want a 40% margin', you cannot just add 40% to cost. Divide the cost by (1 - margin). For a cost of 360 and a 40% margin: price = 360 / (1 - 0.40) = 600. Check: profit = 600 - 360 = 240, and 240 / 600 = 40%. Adding 40% to cost would give 504, which is a margin of only 28.6%.

Our bakery loaf has a variable cost of 500 and sells at 800. Profit before fixed costs is 300 per loaf, a margin of 37.5%. This number, called the contribution, pays the fixed costs first and only then becomes real profit.

list: Cost-plus pricing: add a profit amount to your cost. Simple, but ignores customers.
Market pricing: look at what similar sellers charge, then decide if you are cheaper, equal or better.
Value pricing: charge more because your product saves time or has higher quality, if customers agree.

body.tip: Do not cut your price just to win customers without checking the effect. In the next lesson you will see how a lower price can force you to sell many more units just to break even.

body.p: The break-even point is the number of units you must sell so that total income equals total costs: no profit, no loss. Every sale beyond it adds profit. Knowing it tells you if a plan is realistic before you spend any money.

body.code:
Contribution per unit = price - variable cost per unit
Break-even units = fixed costs / contribution per unit
Break-even sales value = break-even units x price

body.p: Fixed costs 33,000, price 800, variable cost 500. Contribution = 800 - 500 = 300 per loaf. Break-even = 33,000 / 300 = 110 loaves a month. In money, 110 x 800 = 88,000 naira of sales.
Check it: 110 loaves earn 110 x 800 = 88,000. Costs are 33,000 + 110 x 500 = 88,000. They match, so profit is zero. At 200 loaves, profit = 200 x 800 - 133,000 = 27,000 naira.
Suppose you want 24,000 naira profit a month. Add it to the fixed costs: (33,000 + 24,000) / 300 = 190 loaves.

list: A lower price. At 700 the contribution is 200, so break-even rises to 33,000 / 200 = 165 loaves.
Higher ingredient cost. If the variable cost rises to 550 at price 800, contribution is 250 and break-even is 33,000 / 250 = 132 loaves.
Lower fixed costs, for example sharing a space, lowers the break-even.

body.p: Then ask the honest question: can I really sell that many in a month? If the area has about 80 customers who might buy, a break-even of 110 is a warning sign.

body.tip: A break-even figure is only as good as your cost numbers. Update it whenever prices of your supplies or rent change.

body.p: Marketing means helping the right people know you exist and want to buy. It does not need a big budget. Start with your customer sentence from lesson one and go where those people already are.

list: Word of mouth: do good work and ask happy customers to tell two friends.
A phone number and a clear name on a sign, a bag or a social media page.
Photos of your real products, with the price shown.
Samples or a small trial for new customers.
Reliable service: opening when you say you will and keeping promises about time.

body.p: Records show whether you are really making money. A basic notebook or spreadsheet with the date, what was sold, amount received, and every cost paid is enough. Keep receipts. Do this every day, not once a month from memory.

body.code:
Weekly record (money units)
Sales ............................ 84,000
Cost of goods sold ............... 51,000
Share of rent and other fixed .... 9,000
Profit = 84,000 - 51,000 - 9,000 = 24,000

body.p: If business cash pays for family needs with no note, you cannot tell if the business is working. Pay yourself a fixed amount, like a small wage, on a set day. Put business money in a separate wallet, mobile money account or bank account if possible. If you must take extra, write it down as a 'drawing' so the record stays correct.

steps: Choose a weekly or monthly 'wage' for yourself based on your profit records.
Move that amount to your personal wallet on the same day each period.
Leave the rest in the business for stock, rent and savings.
Review once a month: are sales above your break-even?

body.tip: Check your country's rules on registering a business, keeping accounts and paying tax. The rules and rates differ widely, so get current information from official sources.

lessons.title: When and how to ask for help

body.p: No founder knows everything. Asking for help early is cheaper than fixing a big mistake later. The skill is knowing what to ask, whom to ask, and how to avoid people who will take advantage.

list: You cannot work out your costs, prices or break-even and your records do not make sense.
You must sign a contract, lease or loan and do not understand every clause.
You are unsure about registration, licences or tax obligations in your country.
Your sales are falling and you do not know why.
You are thinking about borrowing money.
An experienced local business owner: ask for 30 minutes and prepare questions.
Your school, university or community enterprise or careers office.
A government, non-profit or community small-business support service, where one exists.
A qualified accountant or adviser for accounts and tax questions, for a fee agreed in advance.
Family, friends and customers for honest feedback.

body.p: Before you borrow, check that the business can repay. Suppose you borrow 60,000 and must repay 66,000 in total over 6 months. Monthly repayment = 66,000 / 6 = 11,000. If your profit after paying yourself is only 8,000 a month, you cannot afford it. Compare the repayment with your profit records, not with your hopes. Make sure you know the total repayment, every fee, and what happens if you pay late.

Be careful with anyone who promises quick riches, asks for money in advance for a 'loan' or 'grant', or pressures you to sign now. Real support organisations are happy to let you read and think first.

steps: Write down the exact question you need answered.
Collect your numbers: costs, prices, sales and records.
Ask two different people and compare their answers.
Decide, and write down the reason so you can learn from the result.

body.tip: Say thank you and tell your helper what you did next. People help again when they see their advice mattered.

quiz.q: A kiosk sells a snack. For each portion the owner pays 250 for ingredients, 90 for oil, 45 for a box and 35 for fuel. What is the variable cost per portion?
Which of these is a fixed cost for a hair salon?
options: The monthly rent of the shop
Hair extensions bought for each customer
Electricity used per hour of drying
Gloves used for each customer

quiz.q: A business has fixed costs of 45,000 a month and a variable cost of 600 per unit. What is the total cost of making 300 units?
A trader buys an item for 600 and sells it for 800. What is the profit margin?
An item costs 400 and sells for 500. What is the markup on cost?
A seller's item costs 360 and she wants a 40% profit margin on the selling price. What price should she charge?
Fixed costs are 45,000 a month. The price is 900 and the variable cost is 600 per unit. What is the break-even number of units?
Using the same business (fixed costs 45,000, price 900, variable cost 600), what is the break-even sales value in money?
The same business wants a profit of 30,000 a month. How many units must it sell?
The variable cost rises from 600 to 650 while the price stays 900 and fixed costs stay 45,000. What is the new break-even number of units?
The business (fixed 45,000, price 900, variable cost 600) sells only 120 units in a month. What is the result?
options: A loss of 9,000
A profit of 9,000
A loss of 30
A loss of 45,000

quiz.q: You have an idea for a food stall. What is the cheapest sensible first step?
options: Rent a shop for a year to look serious
Borrow money for equipment before asking anyone
Sell a small trial batch to likely customers and count real purchases
Assume that friends who say 'good idea' will all buy

quiz.q: A shop owner takes money from the till whenever the family needs it and writes nothing down. What is the main problem?
options: She will pay less tax in every country
Customers will pay higher prices
Records are only needed by banks
She cannot tell whether the business is really making a profit

quiz.q: A weekly record shows sales 84,000, cost of goods 51,000 and share of rent and other fixed costs 9,000. What is the profit?
You ask 20 likely customers and 14 say they would buy at your price. What is the percentage who said yes, and what should you remember?
options: 70%; the result is certain, so borrow and expand now
70%; people are polite, so run a trial to see how many really pay
14%; the number of people asked does not matter
6%; only the people who said no matter
